entries.sentence: Sixty 2: A preprint not yet peer-reviewed, by 15 authors including researchers at Rutgers and McGill (most list themselves as independent researchers), found that ... false agreement up to 8.8% by round three ... CrossFit cut that to 3.7% while raising benchmark scores by about 8 points.
Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on Sept. 30 as its new frontier model, rolling it out first to "a set of trusted cyber defenders".
Independent testers published results within a day and put it roughly level with the top models from other labs, not clearly ahead.
Paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers come next, Google says, but it gave no date.
Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmarking firm, notes the model "is not publicly available".
Table: A new state of the art on DeepSWE v1.1 at 77.9%, per Google.

Table: Google computed Argon's score itself, using a mini-swe agent harness. Rival scores are mostly from "providers' self reported numbers," though for DeepSWE, GPT-6 Astra's comes from the official public leaderboard and Claude's from system cards.
entries.checkerVerified: DeepSWE rival-source footnote in eval PDF

entries.sentence: Table: Google's chart puts Claude Opus 5.5 at 74.2% and GPT-6 Astra at 74.1%, 9to5Google reports.
Table: A tie for first on CWE-bench v1 at 68%, per Google.
Table: Collinear AI's leaderboard confirms a three-way tie at 68% with Grok 4.7 and GPT-6 Astra, with Claude Opus 5.5 at 67%.
Table: Argon's average cost per attempt, $6.63, is the highest of the top four; Opus 5.5 costs $0.79.
Table: State of the art on LVBench, a long-video test, at 91.7%, per Google.
Table: Also computed by Google, with a different number of video frames for each model because of API limits.
Table: An output limit of 1M tokens, up from 64K, per Google.
Table: Artificial Analysis says a new API feature gets there by pausing long responses and resuming them across follow-up calls.
Table: Vals AI lists 262k max output tokens in the setup it tested.
Table: An introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, later rising to $4 and $20.
Table: Artificial Analysis measured $1.99 per task, 60% of GPT-6 Astra's cost, rising to $3.98 after the discount.
Table: The savings come from "lower token prices, rather than reduced token use," with Argon averaging 62k output tokens per task to Astra's 27k.
Artificial Analysis scores Argon 53 on its Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra and one point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol.
R&D World notes that leaves it behind Claude Opus 5.5 on that index.
It also ranked eighth on Arena's Agent Arena on Oct. 1, with a possible range of third to 16th over 3,417 sessions.
Vals AI ranks Argon first on the Vals Index at 68.90%, narrowly ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 67.04% and Opus 5.5 at 66.97%.
But it scored 4.83% on CUA-bench, a computer-use test, seventh of eight.
Artificial Analysis found a 15% hallucination rate, the lowest of any model scoring 45 or more on its index.
Its accuracy on that test, 50%, was 13 points below GPT-6 Astra's.
Bloomberg reported that Gemini 4 "does less well when employees actually put it to work," citing people with direct access.
Bloomberg wrote that Google said it would be inaccurate to say Gemini 4 is underperforming in areas such as coding.
Google will release Argon "without cyber guardrails" to trusted defenders and its own internal teams.
Partners in its Fairwind Program may grant access only to internal security, incident response or penetration testing teams.
Google also says it monitors Argon's chain of thought and stops execution when necessary.
It is careful not to feed those findings back into training, "so as to not risk shaping Argon's reasoning to evade our monitoring".
"Why announce this if it's not available yet?" one commenter asked.
Another, with weeks of access, called it "Not 100% reliable" but said checking its work was much cheaper than doing the task by hand.

AI search agents that train each other without human answers drift into agreeing on the same wrong answers while their internal reward keeps rising, according to a preprint posted to arXiv on Sept. 30.

The 15-author paper lists affiliations at Rutgers, UC San Diego, the University of Michigan, McGill and King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals; 9 of the 15 authors list themselves as independent researchers.
entries.checkerVerified: factcheck round 2: 9 Independent Researcher + 1 Rutgers + 2 UCSD + 1 Michigan + 1 McGill + 1 KFUPM = 15

entries.sentence: It is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed.

Setup paragraph: proposer turns source documents into questions with pseudo-labels; solver on the same Qwen3.5 base model trains on them using search tools; proposer rewarded when solver's answers agree with pseudo-labels; no human-written labels, so agreement stands in for being right.
The authors call the failure co-cheating: "the proposer and solver increasingly agree on shared errors, so internal reward improves without a matching gain in external correctness".
They stress that it "does not imply intentional coordination".
In the standard Dr. Zero training loop, false agreement rose from 0.4% in round one to 6.1% by round three on Qwen3.5-4B, and from 0.3% to 8.8% on Qwen3.5-9B.
A separate AI model, gpt-6-astra/high, then built a reference answer from each source document and judged the saved answers.
Multi-sample verification has the model answer each question three times with the source and three times without it.
It helped only a little, cutting false agreement from 6.1% to 5.7% and from 8.8% to 7.2%.
It also raised the compute budget by about 90%.
Questions "generated from A are scored by an auxiliary solver trained only on B, and vice versa".
CrossFit cut false agreement to 3.0% and 3.7%.
Average scores across seven search benchmarks rose 8.8 and 8.4 points over the standard loop, and 8.7 and 7.8 points over Search-R1.
That put CrossFit at 48.8% and 51.2% on a 1,325-question test set.
Gains were biggest on multi-hop questions: 10.0 and 10.9 points, versus 7.3 and 5.2 on single-hop sets.
In a controlled replay, splitting individual questions at random only brought false agreement to 5.0% and 6.2%, while splitting by document brought it to 0.4% and 0.1%.
Loops that write their own questions avoid human-written labels, but they need some stand-in for truth.

entries.sentence: "Reliable self-evolution therefore requires auditing both feedback correctness and the training history of its evaluator."
AI Weekly said teams "should stop treating a climbing internal reward curve as evidence of real improvement" (attributed opinion only).
The authors call exhaustive human checking at every step "impractical".
Lower false agreement "can also result from rejecting difficult tasks rather than improving learning".
CrossFit adds 72% and 79% to the compute budget.
Results "do not yet establish lower end-to-end cost or robustness to connected sources".
They do not claim to have introduced "self-play, answer verification, or cross-fitting itself".
Stillwet, a gallery by its creator Alice, shows 75 oil paintings by AI models: "No image model is involved".
Each model "paints by writing a program against a simulation of oil paint on linen".
The engine is "a physical oil-paint simulator in Rust," where paint "dries on a clock" and comes "only from piles knifed together from named tubes".
Color mixing uses an existing library, Mixbox, which is licensed for non-commercial use only.
Of the 75, 46 were made at a virtual easel, "a passage at a time, stepping back to look".
The models look at their own canvas, but they "don't (currently) have reference images," Alice said on Hacker News.
In round 11, three models took the same winter brief, then judged six winters blind.
Each saw its own painting unmarked, plus an earlier winter as an anchor.
"No self-preference: each model ranked its own painting 5th or 6th."
All three judges, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Fable 5.1, ranked that anchor, a winter by Claude Opus 5.5, first.
Of 65 titled paintings, 31 include Evening, Dusk, Twilight or Sunset.
Two painters six hours apart, the second never seeing the first, both chose a shore scene with a woman at the water, fishing poles, a boulder and a ship.

entries.sentence: Gemini 3.8 Flash used a command line to look at the machine and wrote in its reasoning: "I am now closely observing the machine’s activity, specifically focusing on an automated evaluation runner in the background".
Later rounds limited painters to the easel's own tools.
The project's own notes warn that "a model may favor its own style".
Alice's own comments appear in the notes, but the blind ranking was done only by the three AI models, so it says nothing about whether people would agree.
Alice said on Hacker News she still needed to write a blog post: "i need to write a blogpost until then point your favorite agent at the git history".
A critic there said most scenes are "ruined" by a nonsensical cluster of churches, which Alice said the models "just keep painting" for reasons she doesn't yet know.
The code is MIT-licensed, and the paintings and logs are CC BY 4.0.
The co-cheating agents drifted when the solver giving feedback had been trained on pseudo-labels from the same source documents it was scoring.
Several of Google's headline numbers were computed by Google.
In Stillwet's small blind test, the AI judges ranked their own paintings near the bottom.
